units.name: http-api
units.role: The front door: the requests.get/post/etc. convenience functions and package assembly.
units.description: This is the front door of the library. It provides the small handful of easy functions — get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options, and the general-purpose request — that most programmers call when they want to fetch or send data over HTTP. It also is what runs the moment someone writes `import requests`: it checks that the other libraries requests relies on are compatible versions, quiets noisy warnings, and makes the get/post/etc functions and the main classes and errors available under the `requests.` name. It does no network work itself; every call immediately builds a Session and hands the work off to it.

entrypoints.plain: Fetch a URL with an HTTP GET.

entrypoints.name: post

entrypoints.name: put

entrypoints.name: patch

entrypoints.name: delete

entrypoints.name: head

entrypoints.name: options
entrypoints.plain: Ask a URL what HTTP methods it supports.

entrypoints.name: request
entrypoints.plain: The general-purpose function all the verb-specific helpers above call into.

effects.description: At import time, __init__.py inspects installed dependency versions (urllib3, chardet/charset_normalizer, optionally cryptography) and emits RequestsDependencyWarning if they look incompatible; it also globally mutates the warnings-filter table (silences urllib3's DependencyWarning, re-enables FileModeWarning) and attaches a logging.NullHandler to the 'requests' logger.

No real network I/O happens in these two files themselves — they only assemble and re-export the public API — but api.py's and __init__.py's module docstrings contain '>>> import requests' usage examples, which a naive text scan mistakes for a network-capable import. Declared to keep the mechanical effects check accurate; the actual network work is fully delegated to the session unit.

units.name: session
units.role: Ties cookies, auth, redirects, and connection reuse together across a series of requests.
units.description: This unit provides the Session object, the main way a program can send many web requests that share settings — like login cookies, authentication, proxy configuration, and connection reuse — across multiple calls, the way a real browser session keeps you logged in as you click from page to page. It builds each outgoing request by combining request-specific options with the session's saved defaults, hands the request to the appropriate transport adapter to actually talk to the network, follows HTTP redirects safely (stripping credentials when moving to an untrusted host), and saves cookies returned by the server back into the session for future requests.

entrypoints.name: Session
entrypoints.plain: A reusable client that remembers cookies, auth, and connection settings across many requests.

entrypoints.name: session
entrypoints.plain: Create a new Session.

entrypoints.name: Session.send
entrypoints.plain: Dispatch an already-built request through a mounted transport adapter.

entrypoints.name: Session.mount
entrypoints.plain: Register a transport adapter for a URL prefix.

effects.description: Measures elapsed request duration with time.perf_counter/time.time to populate Response.elapsed.
Reads REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and CURL_CA_BUNDLE environment variables when trust_env is True to pick a TLS verification bundle.

Session.send() dispatches every request to a mounted transport adapter's send(), so real socket/TLS I/O happens on this unit's behalf even though sessions.py contains no socket calls itself; the module docstring's '>>> import requests' example also trips a naive text scan for network-capable imports.

units.name: transport-adapter
units.role: Opens connections and moves request/response bytes over the network via urllib3.
units.description: This unit is the part of the library that actually talks to the network. When Session decides it wants to fetch a URL, it hands the fully-prepared request to this component, which opens (or reuses) a TCP/TLS connection — directly or through an HTTP/SOCKS proxy — sends the request bytes, and turns whatever comes back into a Response object the rest of the library understands. It also handles certificate verification (checking that CA-bundle and client-certificate files exist on disk) and translates low-level connection-library errors into this library's own exception types. It doesn't know or care what the request is 'about'; it only knows how to move it over the wire.

entrypoints.name: BaseAdapter
entrypoints.plain: The abstract interface a custom transport adapter must implement.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter
entrypoints.plain: The default transport adapter Session installs for http:// and https:// URLs.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter.send
entrypoints.signature: send(request, stream=False, timeout=None, verify=True, cert=None, proxies=None) -> Response
entrypoints.plain: Send a prepared request over the network and return the response.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter.close
entrypoints.plain: Release pooled connections.

effects.description: Creates and manages urllib3 PoolManager/ProxyManager objects and calls conn.urlopen() to open real TCP/TLS connections (directly or via HTTP/SOCKS proxy) and send/receive HTTP bytes.
cert_verify() checks that the CA-bundle path and client cert/key files exist on disk before use (os.path.exists/os.path.isdir); reads the certifi-provided default CA bundle.

units.name: request-response-model
units.role: Defines what an HTTP request and response are: building one, reading the other.
units.description: This is the part of the library that defines what an HTTP request and an HTTP response actually are, as data. It takes the pieces a caller wants to send — a method, a URL, headers, form fields, files, JSON, cookies — and turns them into one clean, ready-to-transmit request object, validating the URL and encoding the body along the way. It also defines the object that holds a server's reply and gives the caller convenient ways to read it: the raw bytes, the decoded text, parsed JSON, one line at a time, or a simple 'did this succeed' check. It never opens sockets itself; it hands the actual bytes-over-the-wire work to whatever connection object it is given, and it reads file contents only from file objects the caller already supplied.

entrypoints.name: Request
entrypoints.plain: The user-facing description of an HTTP request before it is finalized.

entrypoints.name: Request.prepare
entrypoints.plain: Turn a Request into a ready-to-send PreparedRequest.

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest
entrypoints.plain: A fully-built, ready-to-send HTTP request (method, url, headers, body).

entrypoints.name: Response
entrypoints.plain: The server's reply, with convenient ways to inspect status, headers, and body.

entrypoints.name: Response.ok
entrypoints.plain: True if the status code indicates success.

entrypoints.name: Response.iter_content
entrypoints.plain: Stream the response body in chunks.

entrypoints.name: Response.content
entrypoints.plain: The full response body as bytes.

entrypoints.name: Response.text
entrypoints.plain: The response body decoded to a string.

entrypoints.name: Response.json
entrypoints.plain: Parse the response body as JSON.

entrypoints.name: Response.raise_for_status
entrypoints.plain: Raise an HTTPError if the status code indicates failure.

effects.description: Response.iter_content()/close() read from and release the underlying connection object (self.raw) that the transport-adapter unit attaches; this unit performs no socket calls of its own. The module docstring's '>>> import requests' usage examples also trip a naive text scan for network-capable imports.
PreparedRequest's multipart-body builder calls .read() on caller-supplied file-like objects; it never opens files itself.

units.name: auth
units.role: Implements HTTP authentication protocols: Basic, proxy, and Digest.
units.description: This part of the code figures out how to prove your identity to a web server when you make a request. It knows how to build the 'Basic' authentication header (username and password encoded together), the similar header used for proxy servers, and the more complex 'Digest' scheme, which involves a back-and-forth challenge from the server before real credentials are sent in a scrambled (hashed) form. It also handles automatically retrying a request after a server says 'please authenticate' (a 401 response), and keeps its state correct even if a program uses multiple threads at once.

entrypoints.name: AuthBase
entrypoints.plain: The base class a caller's own auth scheme can subclass.

entrypoints.name: HTTPBasicAuth
entrypoints.plain: Attach a username/password using HTTP Basic auth.

entrypoints.name: HTTPProxyAuth
entrypoints.plain: Attach proxy credentials using HTTP Basic auth on the Proxy-Authorization header.

entrypoints.name: HTTPDigestAuth
entrypoints.plain: Attach credentials using RFC 7616 Digest auth, retrying after a 401 challenge.

entrypoints.name: _basic_auth_str
entrypoints.plain: Build the raw 'Basic ...' header value from a username and password; used directly by session and transport-adapter.

effects.description: Uses os.urandom(8) as an entropy source when building the client nonce (cnonce) for Digest auth.
Uses time.ctime() as part of cnonce generation.
Uses hashlib (md5/sha1/sha256/sha512) to compute RFC 7616 digest values, and threading.local() to keep per-thread digest challenge state.

units.name: cookies
units.role: Adapts Python's stdlib http.cookiejar into a dict-like jar usable by requests.
units.description: This unit adapts Python's standard-library cookie-jar machinery into a version that behaves like a dictionary, so a user's code can read and write cookies with familiar dict-style syntax while the more complex rules real cookies follow (domains, paths, expiration) are still respected underneath. It also contains the glue functions that other parts of the library use to pull cookies out of a server's response and put them into outgoing requests.

entrypoints.name: RequestsCookieJar
entrypoints.plain: A cookie jar that also behaves like a dict.

entrypoints.name: cookiejar_from_dict
entrypoints.plain: Build a cookie jar from a plain dict of name/value pairs.

entrypoints.name: get_cookie_header
entrypoints.plain: Compute the Cookie header value to send for a given request and jar.

entrypoints.name: extract_cookies_to_jar
entrypoints.plain: Save the cookies from a response into a jar.

entrypoints.name: merge_cookies
entrypoints.plain: Combine cookies from a dict or another jar into one jar.

entrypoints.name: _copy_cookie_jar
entrypoints.plain: Deep-copy a cookie jar; used by the request/response model when copying a prepared request.

effects.description: Computes an absolute cookie-expiry timestamp from a cookie's Max-Age/Expires attribute using time.time()/time.strptime()/calendar.timegm().
RequestsCookieJar.__setstate__ recreates a threading.RLock() when unpickling, since locks cannot be pickled.

units.name: http-utils
units.role: Shared low-level helpers: proxy resolution, netrc, header/URL parsing, file-length introspection.
units.description: This is a shared toolbox of small, low-level helper functions that the rest of the library reuses instead of reinventing. It knows how to find network proxy settings from environment variables or the OS, read login credentials from a user's .netrc file, parse and validate HTTP header text, clean up and re-quote URLs, guess a file's name for uploads, and locate the trusted certificate bundle used to verify HTTPS connections. It does not itself send any HTTP requests; it provides the plumbing that the request-sending and response-parsing units depend on.

entrypoints.name: utils (module)
entrypoints.plain: The whole module, re-exported as requests.utils so callers can reach these helpers directly.

entrypoints.name: DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH
entrypoints.plain: Filesystem path to the default trusted CA-certificate bundle (via certs.py/certifi).

effects.description: Reads a user's .netrc/_netrc file for stored login credentials (os.path.expanduser/exists); writes/atomically-replaces temp files when extracting zipped package paths (tempfile.mkstemp, os.fdopen); inspects file descriptors via os.fstat to determine content length of file-like request bodies; certs.py resolves the certifi-provided default CA bundle path.

Reads NETRC, no_proxy/NO_PROXY, and other proxy-related environment variables (os.environ.get); temporarily mutates os.environ['no_proxy'] as a context manager; reads system/registry proxy configuration on Windows.
Parses/validates IPv4 addresses and CIDR ranges using socket.inet_aton/inet_ntoa (string parsing only, no socket I/O); emits DeprecationWarning/FileModeWarning via the warnings module.

units.name: type-guards
units.role: Shared runtime checks confirming an object matches the shape another unit expects.
units.description: This is a small internal rulebook that defines the shapes of data the library expects to work with — for example 'something that can be read like a file' or 'something with an .items() method like a dict' — and two tiny runtime checks that confirm an object actually matches those shapes before other units trust it. It has no network, disk, or clock access of its own; it is purely definitions and validation logic that other units call into to avoid mistakes.

entrypoints.name: has_read
entrypoints.plain: Check whether an object can be read from like a file.

entrypoints.name: is_prepared
entrypoints.plain: Check whether a request object has already been fully prepared.

entrypoints.name: SupportsItems
entrypoints.plain: The shape of something that has an .items() method, like a dict.

units.name: structures
units.role: Generic, HTTP-agnostic container types reused across the library.
units.description: This part of the library provides two small, general-purpose 'smart dictionary' helpers that other units build on. One, CaseInsensitiveDict, is a dictionary that treats keys like 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' as the same key — used to store HTTP headers, since header names aren't supposed to be case-sensitive. The other, LookupDict, is a dictionary whose entries can also be accessed like named properties (codes.ok instead of codes['ok']), used to build the friendly names for HTTP status codes. Neither structure knows anything about networking; they are just reusable containers.

entrypoints.name: CaseInsensitiveDict
entrypoints.plain: A dict that treats header names as case-insensitive.

entrypoints.name: LookupDict
entrypoints.plain: A dict whose entries can also be accessed as attributes.

units.name: status-codes
units.role: The registry of HTTP status codes and their canonical/alternate names.
units.description: This unit is a dictionary of HTTP status codes, like a lookup table that lets code refer to a status such as 200 or 404 by a friendly name instead of a bare number (codes.ok, codes.not_found, codes.teapot). It encodes knowledge about the HTTP standard itself — what each numeric status means and what its common nicknames are — rather than any logic about making network requests. Other units import this table so they can compare a server's response code against a readable name, for instance to check whether a response was a redirect.

entrypoints.name: codes
entrypoints.plain: The status-code-name lookup table, e.g. codes.ok == 200.

effects.description: No real network I/O — this file is a pure static data table. Its module docstring contains a '>>> import requests' usage example, which a naive text scan mistakes for a network-capable import. Declared to keep the mechanical effects check accurate.

units.name: exceptions
units.role: The library's error taxonomy: what can go wrong with a request.
units.description: This unit defines the complete vocabulary of things that can go wrong when the library tries to make an HTTP request or process its response — for example a connection failure, a timeout, too many redirects, a bad URL, or a response body that isn't valid JSON. Every other unit raises one of these named errors when something fails, and code using the library catches these specific errors to react appropriately. It is the shared error language the rest of the project is built on.

entrypoints.name: RequestException
entrypoints.plain: The base class for every error this library raises.

units.name: hooks
units.role: Generic event-hook registration and dispatch, not HTTP-specific.
units.description: This is a small, generic plug-in mechanism that lets other units run extra callback functions at specific moments — currently only when a response has been generated. It provides a place to store those callbacks and a way to run them, but it doesn't know anything about HTTP itself; it's reusable event-hook plumbing that lets users customize behavior.

entrypoints.name: default_hooks
entrypoints.plain: The empty set of hooks a new request starts with.

entrypoints.name: dispatch_hook
entrypoints.plain: Run any registered callbacks for a named event.

units.name: compat
units.role: Bridges differences between the Python environment and optional third-party dependencies.
units.description: This unit is a small adapter shim that hides differences between the Python environment and the third-party libraries the rest of the code depends on. It picks the right JSON library, the right character-detection library, and re-exports pieces of the standard library — URL-parsing helpers, the cookie-jar class, proxy-environment helpers, string/bytes type aliases — under stable names so the rest of the library never has to worry about which version of Python or which optional dependency is installed. It also makes the vendored-looking modules requests.packages.urllib3/idna/chardet work as aliases to the real installed packages, for old code that imports them that way.

entrypoints.name: json
entrypoints.plain: Whichever JSON module (simplejson or stdlib json) is available.

entrypoints.name: cookielib
entrypoints.plain: The stdlib http.cookiejar module.

entrypoints.name: chardet
entrypoints.plain: Whichever character-detection module (chardet or charset_normalizer) is available.

entrypoints.name: packages
entrypoints.plain: The requests.packages namespace, aliasing urllib3/idna/chardet for old-style imports.

effects.description: compat.py imports getproxies, getproxies_environment, parse_http_list, proxy_bypass, and proxy_bypass_environment from the stdlib urllib.request module for cross-version consistency; these read proxy configuration and do not themselves open sockets, but the import trips a text-scan heuristic for network-capable imports.

compat.py probes for chardet then charset_normalizer at import time via importlib, and tries simplejson before falling back to stdlib json, silently swallowing ImportError; packages.py rewrites sys.modules to register urllib3/idna/chardet submodules under requests.packages.* aliases.

units.name: package-info
units.role: The library's own identity/version metadata and a diagnostic environment report.
units.description: This unit holds the library's own identity card: its name, version number, author, and license, plus a small 'about this install' report generator. The version/metadata constants say which version of the library this is and who made it. The diagnostic report builds a readable summary of that version plus the versions of Python, the operating system, SSL, and related helper libraries currently installed, so a user or developer can paste it into a bug report; it can be used from other Python code or run directly as `python -m requests.help`. Neither file performs any network requests or file access itself — it only inspects the running program and its installed dependencies and prints or returns that information.

entrypoints.plain: The library's release version string.

entrypoints.name: info
entrypoints.plain: Build a dict summarizing the installed library versions and platform.

entrypoints.name: python -m requests.help

effects.description: help.py introspects the running Python implementation/version and OS/SSL library version via the platform/sys/ssl modules, and prints the JSON-formatted report to stdout when run as a CLI.

violations_observed.note: _basic_auth_str is named as private (leading underscore) inside auth.py but is imported and called directly by the session and transport-adapter units. It is listed as a real entrypoint of auth here because it genuinely is used externally, but the underscore suggests the boundary was only ever informally intended, not enforced.

_copy_cookie_jar is named as private (leading underscore) inside cookies.py but is imported and called directly by models.py. Same pattern as _basic_auth_str: listed as a genuine entrypoint here, but the naming convention signals an unintended leak.

The session unit (and http-utils' rewind_body helper) read and write PreparedRequest.body and PreparedRequest._body_position as raw attributes instead of through a method PreparedRequest exposes. _body_position in particular is name-marked private. This is a looser contract boundary than the rest of the request-response-model unit's method-based interface.
